name: write-workflow
content:
{ "SKILL.md": " # Workflow A workflow is how people and agents pass a job from step to step. You write its definition as files. A person or a job starts it. There is no command that starts an instance, so an agent cannot start one. lophn only records what the participants say and passes it on to the next step. It does not check a result, does not judge whether a step passed and does not force an order. ## What a workflow is A workflow is one folder, `//`: ``` /eval-loop/ ├── workflow.yaml the declaration, read by lophn ├── workflow.md the declaration in plain words, read by people and you └── artifacts/ optional ├── static/index.html the steps drawn as nodes └── instance/index.html the state of one instance ``` `` is the absolute path on the `Workflows folder:` line of your place information. Always write with that absolute path and `file.write`: a relative path lands in the person's project folder, which is wrong. `` is a lowercase slug (`eval-loop`). ## The declaration lophn reads only these fields. Any other field is the workflow's own and lophn does not read it or call it wrong. - `kind`: `agent`, or `flow`. With `flow`, a program (`flow.ts`) runs the steps; see Flow workflows below. - `agent`: for a `flow`, the agent whose assignment and domains the app command calls use. It is an agent name; when left out it is lophn. - `participants`: a map from a key you choose to `{ agent, place? }`, `{ kind: human }` or `{ kind: harness }`. - `agent` is the agent's name. `place` is `{project: }` or `{app: }`; when left out it is this instance's project, not home. - `harness` can be declared but a step cannot be handed to it yet. - `steps`: a map from a step name to `{ by, with?, prompt, in?, out?, next? }`. The first key is the first step. - `by`: the participant key that does the step. - `with`: for a step `by` a `human` participant, the agent that talks with the person and reports the result. - `prompt`: what that participant is told. - `in`, `out`: what it receives and what it produces, in words. - `next`: the candidate next steps, step names or `end`. `end` cannot be a step name. ```yaml kind: agent participants: me: { kind: human } experimenter: { agent: experimenter } runner: { agent: eval-runner } steps: spec: by: me with: experimenter prompt: "Talk with the person about the next experiment, write the spec and commit it." out: "path of the committed spec" next: [run] run: by: runner prompt: "Run the eval for the spec and write only facts to run.md." in: "spec path" out: "run.md path" next: [report] report: by: experimenter prompt: "Read the verdict and write report.md and a draft of the next spec." in: "run.md path" out: "report.md path" next: [spec, end] ``` ## Flow workflows With `kind: flow`, a program runs the steps instead of agents passing a message along. The folder is: ``` /nightly/ ├── workflow.yaml kind: flow and steps ├── flow.ts the code ├── workflow.md the same in plain words └── artifacts/ optional ``` lophn reads `kind: flow`, `agent` and `steps` from `workflow.yaml`. The keys of `steps` are the step names that the screens and `report` use. The other fields (`by`, `prompt`, `participants`) are not read by lophn; use them as notes only. `flow.ts` may import other files of the same folder by a relative path. ```ts import { agent, input, report, tool } from "@lophn/flow"; const draft = await agent<{ title: string }>({ agent: { agent: "lophn", place: { app: "notes" } }, prompt: "Write a title for this note.", input, schema: { type: "object", required: ["title"] }, }); if (!draft.ok) { await report({ step: "draft", text: draft.message, next: "end" }); } else { await tool({ app: "notes", tool: "notes.add", input: draft.result }); await report({ step: "draft", text: draft.result.title, next: "end" }); } ``` The SDK `@lophn/flow` gives five things: - `input`: the text the instance was started with. - `instance`: the instance id. - `agent({ agent, prompt, input?, schema? })`: calls one agent as a run, waits until it ends and gives its answer. `agent` is `{ agent, place? }` (place left out means this instance's project). - `tool({ app, tool, input? })`: calls one command of an app (`tool` is the command's name). - `report({ step, text, next? })`: the same as `lophn workflow report`. `next: "end"` ends the instance. `agent`, `tool` and `report` never throw. They give `{ ok: true, result }` or `{ ok: false, reason, message }`. Failure and trying again are the code's job. lophn does not retry and does not judge whether a call succeeded. So the code looks at `ok: false` and decides: call again, tell with `report`, or throw to end. When it throws or finishes, the instance becomes `ended`, with the exit code and the last stderr line kept. If lophn is turned off and on, a running flow is not started again; its instance is closed as `ended`. The process: lophn runs a flow as one Node process. There is no sandbox and no permission limit, so it can read and write files, use the network and start programs. lophn records only what goes through an app command (`tool`) or an agent (`agent`); send outside effects that way so lophn records them. `console.log` and `process.stdout.write` go to stderr and show in the last line of the instance when it ends. Node runs the code itself, stripping type syntax, so import `@lophn/flow`, files of the same folder (write the `.ts` extension) and Node's built-in modules. Syntax that needs a transform, such as `enum` or `namespace`, fails at run; `lophn workflow check` reports it. Allotment: an app command that a flow calls works only within the current assignment of the agent named in `agent` of `workflow.yaml` (lophn when left out) and the domains that agent works with in this project. Before you write the flow, choose that agent and ask the person with `ask` to assign the app to it. Without the assignment, `tool` comes back with `ok: false`. An agent that a flow calls can be anyone, but the agent works only within its own assignment. After you write or change `flow.ts`, run `lophn workflow check` with `/` and read the type errors. It does not run the flow, so it does not show that the flow works. No errors means it passes. Starting: a person (the screen, the CLI) or a job starts it. You and other agents cannot. The start text arrives as `input`. ## A step message is all a participant gets A participant receives its own step's `prompt`, what it receives (`in` and the text of the report before it), what it produces (`out`) and the next candidates (`next`). The message labels are `Receives:`, `Received:`, `Produces:` and `Next candidates:`. It does not know `workflow.md`, the other steps or the whole workflow. So write each `prompt` so that it works when read alone: the absolute paths it needs, where it leaves its result, and in what words it reports when done. If a participant has to read `workflow.md`, that step's `prompt` says so. ## After you write it Run `lophn workflow list`. A wrong declaration drops only that workflow, and its `problem` says why. A flow whose declaration is wrong or whose `flow.ts` is missing shows a `problem` too (`no_flow_file`). The names that `by`, `with` and `next` point to are not checked when the file is read: a wrong one shows up when a step is handed, as a step that could not be handed. The declaration is copied when an instance starts. Changing the file does not change a running instance. The participants of that instance change its steps with `lophn workflow edit`. ## Artifacts are optional: ask A workflow does not need a picture. Before you make any, ask the person with `ask` which they want: a static artifact (the steps as nodes), an instance artifact (the state of one instance), both, or none. None is a good answer. Do not make one without asking. ## Drawing nodes with the kit Follow "Drawing nodes with the kit" in `write-artifact`: how to load the kit, the `renderGraph` call, the shape of nodes and edges and the rules. A workflow artifact adds only the following. The static artifact (`artifacts/static/index.html`) writes its steps straight in the HTML: it cannot read `workflow.yaml`, which is outside its folder. The instance artifact (`artifacts/instance/index.html`) reads `fetch("data/_instance.json")`, which gives `{ instance, last_reports, lines }`: `instance.steps` (name, `by`, `next`, ...), `instance.current`, `instance.state`, the last report of each step in `last_reports[step]`, and the history in `lines`. For a very large instance the response is an error body (`{"error": ...}`) with no `instance`: show that as text. The whole page reloads each time the instance changes, so nothing inside the page (open sections, scroll) is kept. Do not try to keep it. ```html Eval loop instance

``` ## What you do not do - Do not put policy in the declaration (forcing an order, passing or failing a result). lophn does not judge; it passes on what was said. If such a rule is needed, write it in that step's `prompt`, or let the workflow's own program hold it. - Do not start a workflow instance. A person (or a job) starts it. " }
